title: Exploration and the Columbian Exchange
note: Seeking a sea route to Asian spices, Portugal sailed around Africa and Spain sailed west. Columbus's 1492 voyage linked the hemispheres. The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals, people and diseases both ways; epidemics and conquest devastated Native American societies, and enslaved Africans were forced across the Atlantic.

read.title: Two worlds meet
text: In the 1400s, spices from Asia reached Europe only through many middlemen, which made them costly. Portugal, sponsored by Prince Henry the Navigator, sent caravels down the coast of Africa. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. Spain backed a bolder idea: Christopher Columbus sailed west in 1492, expecting Asia, and landed in the Caribbean instead.

Within decades, Spanish conquistadors had toppled the two largest American empires. Hernán Cortés and thousands of Native allies took the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, in 1521, and Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca Empire in the 1530s. Steel weapons, horses and alliances mattered, but disease mattered most. Smallpox and other illnesses, to which Native Americans had no immunity, killed a large share of the population.

The movement of living things between the hemispheres is called the Columbian Exchange. Maize and potatoes fed growing populations in Europe, Africa and Asia. Horses, cattle and wheat transformed the Americas. American silver from mines such as Potosí flowed into world trade. As Native labor declined, Europeans turned to Africa, and millions of enslaved Africans were carried across the Atlantic on the Middle Passage to work on plantations.
